content: Microwave therapy has been studied as a treatment for cervical ectropion, a condition that is considered normal and not requiring treatment in Western medicine, despite the cervix appearing red and inflamed. However, in China, cervical ectropion is regarded as one of the most common forms of chronic cervicitis. In Chinese medical practice, topical treatments, including microwave tissue coagulation, are frequently employed in hospitals. These treatments are believed to potentially reduce the risk of abnormal metaplasia and infection. The objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness and potential adverse effects of microwave tissue coagulation compared to other treatments or no treatment at all for cervical ectropion. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database (CBM), Chinese Medical Current Contents (CMCC), CAJ Full-text Database, and the Chinese Scientific Journals Database. Additional searches were performed using internet search engines like Google, as well as through reference lists of articles and manual searches of relevant Chinese journals. The search covered all available literature up to May 2009. The inclusion criteria for this study were limited to authentic randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Two independent reviewers contacted the original authors of studies published in China that claimed to be RCTs. They assessed the risk of bias in three identified RCTs and extracted relevant data. However, none of the studies met the participant inclusion criteria outlined in the protocol. Out of 133 studies reported as RCTs, only three were confirmed to be authentic RCTs. Even so, it was unclear whether the participants in these studies were symptomatic before treatment. Furthermore, the methodological quality of these three RCTs was generally poor. No trials were identified that compared microwave therapy to no intervention. Additionally, most of the trials did not evaluate critical outcomes such as symptom relief, quality of life, or patient satisfaction, which are particularly important for women undergoing treatment. While microwave therapy was found to improve the appearance of the cervix compared to laser therapy and interferon-alpha suppository therapy, there was no clear evidence of any other benefits for the women. In conclusion, there is a lack of high-quality RCTs involving symptomatic women with cervical ectropion that compare microwave therapy to other treatments or no treatment. Although microwave therapy may enhance the visual appearance of the cervix, its overall benefits for women remain uncertain.
